metric.why: Five nines, 99.999 percent, allows about five minutes of downtime a year; four nines allows about fifty-two. The gap between marketing nines and contracted, measured, penalty-backed nines is where disputes live.
metric.target: Uptime Institute's tier system (I through IV) is the common design-redundancy vocabulary behind these commitments.
metric.definition: Delivered availability measured against the contracted service level, conventionally quoted in nines.

reading.body:
The difference between four nines and five nines of uptime is roughly forty-seven minutes of tolerated downtime per year, and for AI training jobs that cannot checkpoint and resume, those forty-seven minutes can mean losing days of GPU time.

SLA uptime compliance is not a single fact but a relationship between two numbers: what a data center operator promises and what it actually delivers, measured and penalty-backed. The Uptime Institute's Tier I through Tier IV vocabulary describes the physical redundancy built into a facility, from single-path power and cooling with no fault tolerance at Tier I to fully fault-tolerant infrastructure at Tier IV. A higher tier raises construction cost and, consequently, the cost of the power and space that compute depends on. The tier rating describes design intent, not operational outcome. Delivered availability is the outcome, and the gap between the two is where contractual disputes are resolved.

The data covers the definition, the measurement convention, and the design vocabulary behind these commitments. It does not provide actual compliance figures for any operator, nor does it address how AI workloads specifically affect or are affected by SLA terms. The sibling metrics, UPS battery health and generator runtime, bear directly on whether the physical redundancy promised by a tier rating can actually be sustained during a grid failure, but that relationship is not quantified here.
